alt: A table of the three grades for presenting. Pass: straightforward ideas, an attempt to organise, an attempt to meet the audience’s needs. Merit: challenging ideas with a range of vocabulary, clear structure, achieves the purpose. Distinction: sophisticated ideas and vocabulary, an effective range of engagement strategies, achieves the purpose. Every grade needs audibility and spoken Standard English.
caption: Every criterion for a grade must be met; challenging and sophisticated ideas need depth.

after: ## Choosing a topic with room to grow
alt: Four flat topics become topics with depth: my favourite football club becomes “Should football clubs be owned by their fans?”; climate change becomes what one town can realistically do; social media becomes whether it makes teenagers more or less lonely; a holiday in Italy becomes what living elsewhere taught me about my own town.
caption: A question or claim gives a topic room for challenging ideas.

alt: A funnel with three filters: does the information serve my purpose, will my audience understand it without a long explanation, and is it memorable when heard once? What passes goes into the talk; the rest is cut. One vivid example often beats three statistics, and sources are noted for questions.
caption: Keep only what serves the purpose, suits the audience and sticks when heard once.

alt: Five shapes for a talk: problem and solution; claim, reasons and counter-argument; past, present and future; two options compared; and myth-busting. Then three ways to keep listeners on track: signpost aloud, such as “That brings me to the second”, repeat key ideas, and summarise before concluding.
caption: Listeners cannot reread, so choose a shape and signpost it aloud.

after: ## Spoken style is different from written style
alt: A two-column table. Written style uses long sentences with several clauses, phrases like “It could be argued that…”, parenthesis and headings. Spoken style uses shorter sentences with one idea at a time, “Some people say…”, pauses and separate sentences, and signposting phrases.
caption: Keep a formal register, but write for the ear, not the page.

after: ## Planning for different purposes and audiences
alt: The same talk on volunteering splits two ways. For Year 7 it needs concrete examples and a clear invitation; for governors it needs evidence of benefit and a measured tone. If only the teacher is listening, choose a form such as a radio interview, a pitch to a panel or a speech to a named group.
caption: The audience changes the examples, the evidence and the tone.

after: ## Worked example: planning a Merit-to-Distinction talk
alt: Six numbered steps for a talk on banning cars from the high street on Saturdays: an opening hook describing the street, a spoken signpost, who gains, who loses, a compromise with exemptions and a trial period, and a close that returns to the opening image. Most steps are tagged with the engagement strategy they use.
caption: Challenging ideas, a signposted structure and varied strategies.
